query: AlCrFeNiSi belongs to a high-entropy-alloy family developed to combine properties that traditional single-principal-element alloys often cannot achieve simultaneously. Earlier research sought stable solid solutions and adjusted HEA compositions to target particular properties, but tradeoffs persisted: the CoCrFeMnNi system has limited wear and corrosion resistance, manganese can promote oxidation and oxide spallation, and cobalt-containing systems raise cost and processability concerns. Conventional bulk fabrication can cause compositional segregation during cooling, whereas mainstream metallic additive-manufacturing techniques can generate residual thermal stresses that impair mechanical performance and increase processing complexity. Given cobalt-free AlCrFeNiSi powder feedstock, what single intervention could improve mechanical integrity while limiting segregation, residual stress, and defect formation? State one hypothesis containing the intervention, its causal mechanism, a quantitative or directional outcome relative to conventionally fabricated AlCrFeNiSi, the processing and test boundaries of validity, the prior evidence supporting it, and a decisive experiment that could falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Using an in situ machine-learning-driven closed-loop control system during laser powder bed fusion of cobalt-free AlCrFeNiSi will reduce compositional segregation, residual thermal stresses, and defect (e.g., porosity, hot cracks) formation, thereby enhancing the overall mechanical integrity compared to conventional static process controls.
generation.material_initial_state: Cobalt-free AlCrFeNiSi powder feedstock prepared for laser-based additive manufacturing.
generation.intervention: Implement an in situ machine-learning-driven closed-loop control system that continuously monitors real-time thermal and optical sensor data and adaptively adjusts laser power, scan speed, and scan strategy during processing.
generation.conditions: Laser powder bed fusion processing of AlCrFeNiSi under similar environmental and equipment settings as conventional builds; testing performed under standard post-build mechanical tests (e.g., tensile and hardness tests) and microstructural analyses (e.g., imaging for segregation and defects).
generation.structural_mediator: A more uniform and controlled thermal field during layer-wise deposition that minimizes localized overheating and undercooling.
generation.mechanism: Real-time sensor feedback fed into a machine learning model dynamically modulates laser parameters to control the energy input, which narrows the thermal gradients during rapid melting and solidification. This adjustment suppresses compositional segregation, reduces residual thermal stresses, and limits defect formation such as pores and hot cracks.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to conventional static process parameter controls, the closed-loop system is expected to yield a more homogeneous microstructure with lower defect density and reduced residual stresses, leading to improved tensile strength and ductility. The outcome is expected to be directional (i.e., improved mechanical integrity and reduced defect formation), though the precise magnitude of improvement remains uncertain.
generation.baseline: Conventional laser printing of AlCrFeNiSi using predetermined, static laser parameters that have shown issues with segregation, residual stress, and defect formation.
generation.boundary: Valid for laser powder bed fusion processes using cobalt-free AlCrFeNiSi under parameters and sensor capabilities typical of current industrial additive manufacturing systems; extrapolation beyond these processing conditions or to radically different alloy systems would require further validation.
generation.uncertainty: The exact quantitative improvements in mechanical properties and defect reduction are uncertain until rigorously tested, and the system’s effectiveness may depend on the quality and response time of the real-time sensors and machine learning algorithm performance.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two sets of AlCrFeNiSi samples using laser powder bed fusion: one set employing the in situ machine-learning-driven closed-loop control system and the other using conventional static laser parameter settings. Maintain identical powder batches and environmental conditions for both groups.
measurements: Microstructural analysis via scanning electron microscopy (SEM) and energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) to quantify compositional segregation and defect density.
Residual stress analysis using X-ray diffraction or other non-destructive techniques.
Mechanical testing, including tensile testing and hardness measurements, to assess mechanical integrity.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the closed-loop controlled samples do not show a statistically significant reduction in compositional segregation, residual thermal stresses, and defect density, as well as no measurable improvement in mechanical properties compared to the conventional samples, the hypothesis will be falsified.

AbstractHigh-entropy alloys are known for their promising mechanical properties, wear and corrosion resistance, which are maintained across a wide range of temperatures. In this study, a CoCrFeNiCu-based high-entropy alloy, distinguished from conventional CoCrFeNi systems by the addition of Cu, which is known to enhance toughness and wear resistance, was investigated to better understand the effects of compositional modification on processability and performance. The influence of key process parameters, specifically laser power and scan speed, on the processability of CoCrFeNiCu-based high-entropy alloys produced by laser powder bed fusion additive manufacturing was investigated, with a focus of low laser power, which is critical for minimizing defects and improving the resulting microstructure and mechanical performance. The printed sample density gradually increases with higher volumetric energy density, achieving densities exceeding 99.0%. However, at higher energy densities, the samples exhibit susceptibility to hot cracking, an issue that cannot be mitigated by adjusting the process parameters. Many scholars have studied HEAs [,,], but most focus on design principles, metallurgical mechanisms, phase changes, micro-structures, and properties of HEAs manufactured by conventional technologies. Several AM methods have been successfully implemented to fabricate structures with HEAs []. The powder bed fusion (PBF) processes, specifically the selected laser melting (SLM) technique, have been widely adopted []. SLM is a powder-bed additive manufacturing technology, which is also advantageous for producing complex-shaped parts []. During the SLM process, rapid melting and solidification are attributable to short-time interaction between laser energy and metal powder, which facilitates the formation of fine microstructure and improves the mechanical properties of the parts []. Meanwhile, ultra-fast cooling helps prevent the formation of intermetallic compounds and element dissolution. Thus, SLM was recently also used for HEA manufacturing, and some studies on the manufacturing, microstructure, and tensile properties of these alloys have been reported []. decision.trend: Earlier work on high-entropy alloys via laser-based additive manufacturing (SLM/LPBF) demonstrated that high energy densities can consolidate HEA powders into dense, predominantly single-phase microstructures (PMC6427779). Process optimization efforts on CoCrFeNiMn HEAs highlighted that controlling laser parameters reduces porosity but can induce hot cracking and residual stresses (PMC9736672). For CoCrFeNiCu systems, further optimization of laser scanning speed and power mitigated defects, yet hot cracks and associated thermally driven inhomogeneities remained issues (PMC12250662). Collectively, these studies show that successful reduction of compositional segregation and defects depends heavily on dynamic control of the thermal profile and energy input during layer deposition, but no robust real-time approach has been demonstrated for cobalt-free AlCrFeNiSi feedstocks to simultaneously minimize segregation, residual stress, and pore formation while enhancing mechanical integrity.
decision.unsolved: Despite incremental process innovations, there is no fully resolved method to concurrently suppress compositional segregation, thermal stress accumulation, and defect formation for cobalt-free AlCrFeNiSi builds. Existing parameter optimization often relies on trial-and-error or static process windows that do not account for evolving build conditions. A flexible, data-driven strategy to monitor and dynamically adjust key laser parameters in real-time remains undeveloped for AlCrFeNiSi high-entropy alloys, leaving a critical gap in achieving consistently high mechanical integrity with minimal defects.
decision.lever: Implement an in situ machine-learning-driven closed-loop control system for laser-based 3D printing, which adaptively adjusts parameters (laser power, scan speed, and scan strategy) based on feedback from real-time thermal and optical sensors to reduce thermal gradients, suppress segregation, and limit defect formation in AlCrFeNiSi.
decision.why: Prior studies on SLM and LPBF underscore the importance of carefully modulating energy input to control phase stability, reduce hot cracking, and promote compositional homogeneity. A data-driven, real-time feedback loop can respond instantaneously to process fluctuations, ensuring a more uniform thermal field that optimizes the solidification conditions and minimizes residual stress. This intervention directly addresses the persistent challenges highlighted in previous HEA research—namely segregation and flaws—and it is feasible within the additive manufacturing regime for AlCrFeNiSi powders.
